chapters.title: Chapter 1: Middle Ages in Europe (500-1500 CE)

lessons.title: The Three Phases of the Middle Ages
lessons.notes_html:
The Middle Ages

The Middle Ages in Europe lasted from about 500 CE to 1500 CE. The period began with the fall of the Roman Empire in 476 CE, when Germanic tribes invaded its western part and formed many small kingdoms. Historians divide the Middle Ages into three phases: the Early Middle Ages, the High (Later) Middle Ages and the End of the Middle Ages.

Early Middle Ages

In the early phase, the invading Germanic tribes formed small kingdoms and converted to Christianity. The pope and church leaders became very powerful, and monasteries were the centres of learning. Manorialism became the chief economic system. Charlemagne, king of the Franks, was the most successful king of this phase. Viking invaders attacked many parts of Europe from the 8th to the 10th century CE, and in the 10th century France developed the feudal system to provide security.

High Middle Ages

Conditions improved in the 11th century CE: people grew more nutritious food, health and population improved, towns grew and trade increased. Kings like Henry II of England and Louis IX of France forced feudal lords to accept their authority. Europeans developed the Gothic style of art and architecture, the first universities were founded, and the Crusades were fought (1095-1291 CE). Chengiz Khan founded the Mongol Empire in 1206 CE, and King John signed the Magna Carta in 1215 CE.

End of the Middle Ages

The last phase was a time of trouble. England and France fought the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453 CE), and the Black Death (Bubonic Plague) killed about one-third of the people of Europe between 1347 and 1351 CE. Printing was invented in about 1440 CE, feudalism weakened as Spain, France and England became strong countries, the Renaissance began, and Europeans learnt about America in 1492 CE — the first stage of the modern age.

lessons.title: Kings, Courts and the Power of the Church
lessons.notes_html:
The Coronation

New kings were crowned in a special religious ceremony called a coronation. A leader of the church, such as the pope or a bishop, placed the crown on the king's head. Kings were often anointed with holy oil to show their divine right to rule.

How Kings Came to Power

Kings came to power in different ways. In many cultures the right to rule was in the king's blood: when a king died, his eldest son became king — this is called hereditary succession. If there was no eldest son, a brother or another male relative could become king. In many cases kings were elected by the powerful nobles and lords, and in some countries a council chose the king. Sometimes kings gained power through assassination or by conquering lands in war.

The King's Court

The King's Court meant the king's council and his everyday life. The court travelled with the king wherever he went, so the king could see first-hand what was going on in his kingdom. The king took advice from the wise men of his court — relatives, lords and members of the church — heard the complaints of the people and made decisions. Kings had a special seal to stamp official documents; it proved the document was genuine and worked like the king's signature. When the king visited a place, the local people had to provide food, entertainment and accommodation. No king could rule without the support of his nobles and lords.

The Church and Charlemagne

Christianity played a major role in Europe during the Middle Ages. The Church was an all-powerful force in people's lives; the pope was its head, and the local church was the centre of town life, where weekly ceremonies, marriages and funerals were held. Charlemagne was the leader (king) of the kingdom of the Franks. He united many Christian lands of western Europe and the pope crowned him Emperor of the Romans in the 8th century CE. His name means 'Charles the Great'.

Why 'Dark Ages'?

The early Middle Ages are called the 'Dark Ages' because after the fall of the Roman Empire there was disorder and insecurity: trade and town life declined, and very few people outside the church could read or write, so learning decreased. Monasteries remained the only centres of learning in this dark period.

lessons.title: Daily Life, Agriculture, Trade and Education
lessons.notes_html:
Daily Life

Most people lived in small one- or two-room houses which were very crowded; usually everyone slept in the same room, and family animals such as a cow or horse might also live inside the house. The house was usually dark and smoky from the fire. The local lord lived in a large house called a manor or a castle. Laws fixed the types of clothes each class could wear: peasants wore plain clothes of heavy wool, while the wealthy wore fine wool, velvet and even silk. Peasants ate mostly bread and stew (beans, dried peas, cabbage and other vegetables); meat, cheese and eggs were saved for special occasions.

Agriculture

Agriculture was the main profession of the Middle Ages. Local peasants worked on the land for the lord; they were called the lord's 'villeins', like servants. They worked hard all year long and grew crops such as barley, wheat and oats. Peasants were not allowed to hunt on the lord's land. They also kept gardens with vegetables and fruits, and sometimes a few animals such as chickens and cows.

Trade

Inland trading centres like Milan developed, which passed goods on to the coastal cities for further export. Goods traded between the Arab world and Europe included gold, salt, animal skins, jewels, leather goods, cotton, perfumes, spices and textiles. Merchants travelled far to trade with the people of the Byzantine Empire in southeastern Europe. Medieval trade was slow, carried by ships and animals, and depended on fairs and trading centres rather than modern transport and banking.

Education

There were some schools run by the church where students were taught to read and write Latin. Some children learnt a craft through apprenticeship and the guild system. Very few people attended school; wealthy children often learned through tutors. The first universities began during the Middle Ages — at Bologna, Paris and other cities — where students studied reading, writing, astronomy, mathematics and music.

lessons.title: Art, Literature, Sports and Festivals
lessons.notes_html:
Three Styles of Medieval Art

Middle Ages art can be divided into three main periods and styles. (1) Byzantine Art lacked realism: paintings were flat, with no shadows, the subjects were serious and dark, and almost all were religious; artists focused on symbolism. (2) Romanesque Art was influenced by both Roman and Byzantine art and also focused on religion; it included stained glass, large wall paintings, domed ceilings, carvings, illuminated manuscripts and sculpture. (3) Gothic Art grew out of Romanesque art; Gothic artists used brighter colours, dimensions and viewpoints, and more shadow and light, and tried new subjects. Other art forms included painting, engraving, metal work and stained glass windows.

Literature

The main literature of the Middle Ages was written by religious priests and monks. Famous works include the 'Golden Legend' (stories of the lives of the Saints), 'The Canterbury Tales' by Geoffrey Chaucer, 'The Divine Comedy' by Dante Alighieri, Marco Polo's Travels and the History of the Kings of Britain. Anthems, songs, comedies and philosophical documents about religion were also written.

Sports and Games

Outdoor sports and tournaments added colour to life. Games included playing with ball and bowls, shinty (like hockey), stoolball (like cricket), hammer-throwing, wrestling, horse riding, archery, chess and golf. A knight who proved his fighting abilities in tournaments was often awarded great wealth, and a peasant who performed better was awarded more land, so sports became very popular.

Fairs, Festivals and Feasts

People had no vacations or days off, but they celebrated many festivals. They held fairs, festivals and feasts with lots of eating, music, games and dancing. Most days were special days on the Christian calendar, such as Easter, Christmas and various Saints' days, when the whole village gathered for a feast. These occasions added colour to the hard life of the people.

lessons.title: End of the Middle Ages and Its Legacy
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Issues of the Age

The main issues of the Middle Ages were: insecurity and invasions (Germanic tribes and Viking attacks), the harsh feudal system in which serfs were little better than slaves, poverty and the hard daily life of the peasants, very little education, wars such as the Crusades and the Hundred Years' War, and deadly diseases like the Black Death.

What Caused the End?

Several changes ended the Middle Ages: the Hundred Years' War and the Black Death weakened the old order; feudalism weakened as Spain, France and England became strong countries; the invention of printing (about 1440 CE) spread books and learning; the Renaissance — a time of great learning and art — began; the Ottoman Turks took Istanbul in 1453 CE and ended the Byzantine civilization; and Europeans learnt about America in 1492 CE, which began the modern age.

Important Medieval Inventions

Important inventions of the age changed life forever: the Spinning Wheel made thread and cloth faster; the Compass helped sailors find direction and increased trade and travel; the Printing Press, invented by Johannes Gutenberg in 1440 CE, produced books in great numbers; Eyeglasses helped people with weak eyesight; Gunpowder changed warfare completely; and the Tidal Mill used the power of sea tides to grind grain.

Effect on the Modern World

The Middle Ages laid the foundations of the modern world: the Magna Carta (1215 CE) started the idea that even the king is not above the law and protected the rights of the people; the first universities were founded; the Gothic style enriched art and architecture; inventions such as the printing press, compass, gunpowder and spinning wheel changed life forever; strong national countries emerged as feudalism weakened; and the Renaissance and the discovery of America opened the modern age.

Sources of the Period

Primary sources are the original records made at that time, such as the Magna Carta document (1215 CE), church records, coins, castles, cathedrals and paintings of the age. Secondary sources are books and accounts written later by historians about those events. Comparing both helps a student build a correct picture of the Middle Ages.

lessons.title: The Umayyad Caliphate
lessons.notes_html:
The First Islamic Dynasty

The Umayyad Dynasty was the first Islamic dynasty, ruling from 661 CE to 750 CE. Its founder was Muawiyah-I (602-680 CE), a brilliant Arab general who restored unity to the Muslim empire, made Damascus its capital and reigned from 661 to 680 CE. He set up diwans (government departments) such as the diwan-al-khatam (chancellery) and the bareed (postal service), and expanded the empire to the very gates of Constantinople. Marwan-I (623-685 CE) took over after Muawiyah-II and reigned 684-685 CE, during a civil war and a war against Abdullah Bin Zubair.

A Vast Empire

The Umayyads expanded the Islamic Empire into one of the largest empires in history: it extended from India in the east to Spain in the west, controlling the Middle East, parts of India, much of North Africa and Spain, with a population of around 62 million people — nearly 30% of the world's population at the time.

Advancements

The Umayyads modelled their government on the Byzantines, divided the empire into provinces ruled by governors appointed by the Caliph, and created diwans. Their advancements included a common coinage, Arabic as the official language, standardised weights and measures, a postal service (bareed), and great buildings like the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem and the Umayyad Masjid in Damascus. One of their leaders, Abdul Rahman, escaped to Spain and established his own kingdom at Cordoba, where the Umayyads ruled portions of Spain until the 14th century CE.

Two Great Umayyad Caliphs

Abd-al-Malik Ibn Marwan (647-705 CE), the fifth Umayyad Caliph (685-705 CE), introduced a single Islamic currency in place of Byzantine and Sasanian coinage, made Arabic the language of the bureaucracy, and founded the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. Al-Walid-I (668-715 CE) ruled from 705-715 CE: he allowed Hajjaj Bin Yousaf to conquer Sindh, developed a welfare system, built hospitals and educational institutions, restored Masjid-e-Nabawi in Medina, and built a strong navy.

lessons.title: The Abbasid Caliphate and the Golden Age
lessons.notes_html:
The Abbasids Take Over

The Abbasids vanquished the Umayyad Dynasty in 750 CE because discontent had grown against Umayyad rule — especially among the mawali (non-Arab Muslims), who were treated unequally although Islam teaches equality. Abu Al-Abbas Abdullah Ibn Muhammad as-Saffah became the first Abbasid Caliph (750-754 CE). The Abbasids supported the mawali and moved the capital to Baghdad, founded by Al-Mansur in 762 CE.

The Golden Age of Islam

The early Abbasid period was a time of peace and prosperity called the Golden Age of Islam (about 750-1258 CE). Great advances were made in science, mathematics, medicine and astronomy. Schools for higher education and libraries were built throughout the empire, such as the Bayt-al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad. Arab, Persian and other scholars built on the knowledge they translated from the Greeks and others. The first paper mills were set up in Samarkand, new coins were introduced, and Arabic art and architecture reached new heights.

Two Great Abbasid Caliphs

Al-Mansur (714-775 CE), the second Abbasid Caliph (754-775 CE), founded Baghdad in 762 CE; in his reign literature and scholarly work emerged in full force. Haroon-al-Rashid (763-809 CE), the most famous Abbasid Caliph, ruled from 786 CE to 809 CE. He built a grand palace in Baghdad and established the legendary library Bayt-al-Hikma. Anxious that his people be treated justly, he sometimes disguised himself at night and walked the streets and bazaars to understand the problems of the masses. Other famous figures of the age were Al-Kindi, a great mathematician, and Ibn-al-Haytham, the father of modern optics, who wrote 'Kitab-al-Manazir' (Book of Optics). Umar Ibn Abd-al-Aziz's rule had begun earlier, in 717 CE, in the Umayyad period.

The Fall of the Abbasids

The Abbasid Dynasty fell because of the rise of the Mongol Empire in eastern Asia in the early 12th century CE. In 1258 CE the Mongol ruler Hulagu Khan sacked Baghdad and the Caliph was murdered. The Abbasids fled to Egypt, and the caliphate was re-established at Cairo in 1261 CE, lasting until 1517 CE — but there the Mamluks held the true political and military power, while the Abbasids remained religious leaders.

lessons.title: Muhammad Bin Qasim and the Conquest of Sindh
lessons.notes_html:
The Arrival in 712 CE

The rule of the Muslims in the subcontinent started with the conquest of Sindh by Muhammad Bin Qasim in 712 CE. The immediate cause of his arrival was the looting of Arab ships by pirates of Sindh. When this news reached Hajjaj Bin Yousaf, he sent his nephew Muhammad Bin Qasim to conquer Sindh.

The Conquest

The army under Muhammad Bin Qasim defeated Raja Dahir, who was the Raja of Sindh at that time, and captured the area up to Multan. This happened during the reign of the Umayyad Caliph Al-Walid-I, who had allowed Hajjaj Bin Yousaf to conquer Sindh.

Impacts of the Expedition

Muhammad Bin Qasim played an important role in spreading Islam in the subcontinent: he set up many Masjids and Islamic schools in Sindh and Multan. The Arabs did not force the locals to embrace Islam; many Buddhists and lower-caste Hindus, who lived a miserable and socially segregated life, were impressed by the equality, caste-less system and social justice of the Muslims and embraced Islam. That is why scholars call Sindh the gateway of Islam to other parts of India — his conquest sped up the process of the spread of Islam in the region.

lessons.title: Umayyads and Abbasids Compared
lessons.notes_html:
Similarities

Both dynasties ruled vast empires and spread Islam over large areas of Asia, Africa and Europe. Both were ruled by caliphs with capitals of their own, both set up diwans (government departments), introduced coinage, and built great mosques and buildings. Both used Arabic as the language of the state.

Differences

  • Capital: Damascus (Umayyad) vs Baghdad (Abbasid, founded 762 CE).
  • Period: 661-750 CE (Umayyad, about 90 years) vs 750-1258 CE at Baghdad, then Cairo to 1517 CE (Abbasid).
  • Main fame: the Umayyads are famous for conquest and territorial expansion — from the Indus River to Spain; the Abbasids are famous for learning, science and culture — the Golden Age of Islam.
  • Support base: the Umayyads relied mainly on the Arab nobility, while the Abbasids supported the mawali (non-Arab Muslims) and gave them a share in government.

Islam Spreads Across the World

From the 7th through the 18th centuries CE, Islam spread across the globe. Muslim rulers extended their control throughout North Africa, West Africa and Central Asia. Muslim rulers, soldiers, traders, Sufis, scholars, poets and architects all contributed to shaping a unique Islamic culture. In the subcontinent, Islam entered through Sindh in 712 CE, and in the west it reached Spain in the Umayyad period. In the 7th century CE, Islam also brought a revolution in Arabia itself: the tribal society was united under one faith and one state, idol worship ended, and social justice and equality replaced the old divisions.

lessons.title: The Seljuk and Fatimid Dynasties
lessons.notes_html:
The Seljuk Dynasty

The Seljuk Dynasty was formed in 1037 CE by Tughril Beg (993-1063 CE) and his brother Chaghri Beg. It was a Turkish dynasty based in Central Anatolia; from their homelands near the Aral Sea, the Seljuks advanced first into Khurasan, then into Persia and Anatolia. The Seljuks won the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 CE under Sultan Alp Arslan and conquered most of Anatolia from the Byzantine Empire. Seljuk power reached its zenith under Malik Shah-I, whose vizier was Nizam-ul-Mulk.

Seljuk Contributions

The Seljuks assumed the leadership of the Islamic world by establishing political mastery over the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad. They created a barrier against the Mongol invaders from the East and defended the Islamic world against the Crusaders from the West. They introduced social and political stability, patronised Persian culture, art, literature and language, and Anatolia became Islamized. The madrasas of Sivas and the Mevlana Museum in Konya are notable examples of their architecture. However, their conquest of Anatolia became one of the reasons for the First Crusade (1095-1099 CE); the dynasty was weakened during the first two Crusades, and the Seljuk Empire was invaded by the Mongols around 1194 CE.

The Fatimid Dynasty

Under the Fatimids (909-1171 CE), Egypt became the centre of the empire and Cairo became the most important cultural centre in the Islamic world. Cairo was a major centre for the production of pottery, glass, metalwork, rock-crystal, ivory, wood carving and textiles. Famous Fatimid buildings include the Great Masjid of Mahdiya in Tunisia (916 CE), the Al-Azhar Masjid in Cairo (972 CE) and the Al-Hakim Masjid in Cairo (1013 CE). Fatimid rule was renowned for tolerance: Muslims, Christians and Jews held significant public offices, appointed purely on merit, and women's contributions were valued. The Fatimid Empire collapsed in 1171 CE when Salah-ud-Din Ayubi became the real master of Egypt, overthrew the last Fatimid caliph and established the Ayyubid Dynasty.

lessons.title: The Ayyubids and Salah-ud-Din Ayubi
lessons.notes_html:
Salah-ud-Din Ayubi

Sultan Salah-ud-Din Ayubi (1137-1193 CE) was the founder of the Ayyubid Dynasty in Egypt. He became the real master of Egypt in 1171 CE, overthrew the Fatimid Dynasty and established the Ayyubid Dynasty. He fought for many years against the Crusaders and recaptured the city of Jerusalem in 1187 CE.

Conflict with the Seljuk-linked Zangids

After the death of Nur-ud-Din Zangi, the Ayyubids and the Seljuk-linked Zangids came into conflict over the control of Syria and the Jazira (northern Iraq). The Zangids, successors of Seljuk authority, held Damascus and Aleppo, while Salah-ud-Din extended his rule over Syria, Yemen, Hejaz and northern Iraq in the 12th-13th centuries CE. Thus the Ayyubids replaced Seljuk-linked Zangid rule in Syria, and both Muslim powers competed for leadership against the same Crusader enemy.

Ayyubid Society and Culture

The Ayyubid reign (1171-1260 CE) was an era of social and economic prosperity. Their patronage led to a revival in intellectual activity. In art, the Ayyubids are known especially for inlaid metalwork and ceramics, particularly luster and underglaze-painted wares. They established religious schools and hospitals and introduced public education. Salah-ud-Din and his successors were patrons of art and sciences and issued coins of different types. Cairo's famous Al-Azhar University — founded by the Fatimids — became a leading centre for scholarship and the premier institution of learning in the Muslim world under the Ayyubids. On the whole, Arabic culture and language dominated the Ayyubid Empire.

lessons.title: The Ottoman and Safavid Dynasties
lessons.notes_html:
The Ottoman Dynasty

The Ottoman Dynasty was founded by Osman I, a leader of the Turkish tribes in Anatolia, in 1299 CE. Osman I expanded his kingdom, uniting many independent states of Anatolia under one rule, established a formal government and allowed religious tolerance over the people he conquered. Important Ottoman rulers were Osman I, Orhan, Murad-I and Bayezid-I. In 1453 CE, Mehmed II the Conqueror conquered the ancient city of Constantinople, the Byzantine Empire's capital, and renamed it Istanbul. The Ottoman Dynasty ruled a large portion of the Middle East and Eastern Europe for over 600 years, and was finally dissolved in 1923 CE, becoming the country of Turkey.

The Janissaries

The Janissaries were the famous elite infantry corps of the Ottoman Empire. Many Christian boys were recruited into the Janissary corps; they were given strict military training and discipline, and served as the personal soldiers of the Ottoman Sultan, forming the strongest part of the Ottoman army. Ottoman culture was influenced by Turk, Greek, Roman, Islamic and Persian cultures; its society had a ruling class (the Sultan, his family and high officials) and the reaya (subjects — farmers, merchants and craftsmen).

The Safavid Dynasty

The Safavid Dynasty was founded by Shah Ismail (1487-1524 CE) in 1501 CE. He was crowned at Tabriz, later captured Shiraz, Mesopotamia and Iraq, and thus became master of Najaf and Karbala. The Safavid Dynasty (1501-1736 CE) was one of the most significant ruling dynasties of Iran; it controlled all of present-day Iran, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Armenia, parts of Iraq, Kuwait, Afghanistan and Turkey. Shah Ismail was succeeded by his son Shah Tahmasp-I (1524-1576 CE), who was interested in painting and was a good calligrapher. Safavid rule revived Iran as an economic stronghold between East and West, with an efficient state and bureaucracy based on 'checks and balances'. Persian society was a hierarchy with the Shah at the apex; Persians greatly enjoyed hunting, and the polo-match was a common game.

lessons.title: The Crusades
lessons.notes_html:
What Were the Crusades?

The Crusades were a series of religious wars during the Middle Ages (1095-1300 CE) in which the Christians of Europe tried to regain control of Jerusalem and the Holy Land from the Muslims. They were military expeditions initiated by the medieval papacy. The issues that led to them were: the Christian desire to regain the Holy Land, the advance of the Seljuk Turks in Anatolia, the call of Pope Urban II in 1095 CE, and religious zeal among European Christians.

Main Events

  • First Crusade (1096-1099 CE): After Pope Urban II's call in 1095 CE, European armies marched east; in 1099 CE they captured Jerusalem and set up feudal states (Edessa, Antioch, Tripoli and Jerusalem).
  • Second Crusade (1147-1149 CE): Fought after the city of Edessa was conquered by the Turks in 1146 CE. Sultan Nur-ud-Din Zangi (1118-1174 CE) is regarded as an important figure of this Crusade, and the Crusaders failed to recover Edessa.
  • Third Crusade (1189-1192 CE): Salah-ud-Din Ayubi recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 CE, so the kings of Europe marched again, but they could not retake Jerusalem and made a treaty with Salah-ud-Din.
  • Later Crusades: The Fourth Crusade and the Children's Crusade (1212 CE) also failed, and Muslim rule over the Holy Land continued.

Result

Although the Crusaders failed to hold the Holy Land, the Crusades produced the interest of Europe in trade and commerce with the East, which changed European life in the centuries that followed.

lessons.title: The Delhi Sultanate
lessons.notes_html:
Before the Sultanate

Mahmood Ghaznavi (971-1030 CE) was, according to the book, the first independent ruler of the Ghaznavid Dynasty in Ghazna; he was the son of Sabuktigin, the founder of the dynasty, and he invaded India seventeen times between 1000 CE and 1026 CE. His reasons were political (the Hindu Rajas repeatedly combined against Ghazna), religious (he broke the great idol at Somnath in 1025 CE), economic (the immense wealth of Indian temples and cities) and territorial (he annexed Punjab and made Lahore a centre of his empire). Shahab-ud-Din Muhammad Ghori, born in Ghor in present-day Afghanistan, conquered Lahore in 1186-7 CE, ending Ghaznavid rule; after his victory in the Second Battle of Tarain (1192 CE), Muslim rule was firmly established in northern India.

The Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty

The word 'Mamluk' means a slave. The Mamluk Dynasty was founded by Qutb-ud-Din Aibak (1150-1210 CE), who had been a slave of Muhammad Ghori. Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 CE; the Mamluks ruled Delhi from 1206 to 1290 CE. The greatest Mamluk ruler was Shams-ud-Din Iltutmish, who stopped the attack of the Mongol Emperor Chengiz Khan on India in 1221 CE. Aibak began the Qutb Minar and built masjids, and under the Mamluks Delhi became a great centre of culture.

The Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodhi Dynasties

The Khilji Dynasty, founded by Jalal-ud-Din Firuz Khilji, ruled Delhi from 1290 to 1320 CE. Its most significant ruler was Ala-ud-Din Khilji (1296-1316 CE), who repeatedly defended India against Mongol invasions, built a strong standing army, controlled market prices so common people could buy necessities cheaply, and extended his rule to the Deccan. The Tughlaq Dynasty, founded by Ghias-ud-Din Tughlaq, ruled from 1320 to 1413 CE; then came the Sayyid Dynasty (1414-1451 CE). The Lodhi Dynasty, founded by Bahlul Khan Lodhi, ruled from 1451 to 1526 CE. The last Lodhi ruler, Ibrahim Lodhi, was defeated by Babar in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 CE, which ended the Delhi Sultanate.

lessons.title: Babar, Humayun and Sher Shah Suri
lessons.notes_html:
Babar Founds the Mughal Empire

Zaheer-ud-Din Muhammad Babar (1483-1530 CE) founded the Mughal Empire. The Delhi Sultanate under Ibrahim Lodhi was weak and divided: the Afghan nobles were dissatisfied, and the governor of Punjab, Daulat Khan Lodhi, invited Babar to invade India. Babar defeated and killed Ibrahim Lodhi in the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE) and defeated Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527 CE). His war strategies were: the first effective use of artillery and muskets in the subcontinent; the tulughma tactic, in which cavalry wheeled around the enemy's flanks; carts (araba) chained together as a protective wall for his gunners; a small, well-trained and disciplined army; and careful choice of battlefield. Babar also wrote his famous memories, the Tuzk-e-Babri, and laid out gardens.

Humayun and Sher Shah Suri

After Babar's death, his son Humayun (1508-1556 CE) became emperor. He lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri after defeats at Chausa (1539 CE) and Kannauj (1540 CE) and took exile in Persia. With Persian help he regained Delhi in 1555 CE, restoring Mughal rule, but died in 1556 CE. So Babar's contribution was the founding of the empire, while Humayun's was its restoration.

Reforms of Sher Shah Suri

Sher Shah Suri (1486-1545 CE), founder of the Suri Dynasty, ruled from 1540 to 1545 CE. His contributions were: (1) Roads — he built a highway from Bengal to Kabul, now called the Grand Trunk Road (GT Road), with sarais (rest houses) and shade trees. (2) Postal system — a dak system of horse relays. (3) Land revenue — he got the land measured, fixed the state's share of the produce, and issued patta and qabuliyat to farmers. (4) Currency — he issued a standard silver coin, the rupiya. (5) Administration and justice — he divided his empire into sarkars and parganas and was famous for strict and impartial justice. His reforms later became the model for Akbar's administration.

lessons.title: The Great Mughals: Akbar to Shah Jahan
lessons.notes_html:
Akbar and Sulh-i-Kul

Akbar the Great (1556-1605 CE) made the Mughal Empire great. His famous policy was Sulh-i-Kul, which means 'peace with all'. Its main features were: complete religious tolerance — people of all religions (Muslims, Hindus, Christians, Jains and others) were free to follow their faith; equal treatment of all subjects without discrimination of religion; abolition of the jizya tax on non-Muslims; appointment of talented people of every religion to high posts; and respect for the customs and festivals of all communities. Through Sulh-i-Kul, Akbar united his vast and diverse empire and won the loyalty of non-Muslim subjects, especially the Rajputs. His war strategies included a well-organised army under the mansabdari system, use of artillery and strong forts, swift cavalry campaigns, and diplomacy — marriage alliances and friendships with the Rajputs. After Akbar came Jahangir (1605-1627 CE).

Shah Jahan and Mughal Architecture

The reign of Shah Jahan (1627-1658 CE) is considered the golden period of Mughal architecture. His famous buildings are: (1) The Taj Mahal at Agra, built on the bank of River Yamuna as the tomb of his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal; it is made of white marble, is counted among the Seven Wonders of the World, and has an extensive garden around the tomb. (2) The Red Fort and Jamia Masjid in Delhi. (3) The Shalimar Gardens in Lahore. (4) The Sheesh Mahal in the Shahi Fort of Lahore, decorated with small mirror pieces, and the Nolakha Baradari. (5) The Wazir Khan Mosque in Lahore, famous for its mosaic work and Persian influence. His daughter Jahan Ara also built a congregation masjid in Agra.

Persian Impact

lessons.title: Decline of the Mughals and the War of 1857
lessons.notes_html:
Aurangzeb and the Beginning of Decline

Under Aurangzeb Alamgir (1658-1707 CE) the Mughal Empire reached its largest extent, covering nearly the entire South Asia — the modern-day countries of Pakistan, India and Bangladesh, along with parts of Afghanistan and small parts of Nepal and Myanmar borders. But the factors that led to the crises of the Mughal Dynasty were: Aurangzeb's long Deccan wars against the Marathas, Bijapur and Golconda, which drained the treasury and the army — the book calls his Deccan Policy the beginning of the major downfall of the empire; revolts of the Jats (1669 CE), Sikhs and Rajputs; weak and incapable successors after 1707 CE; the vast size of the empire; and the rising power of the Marathas, who captured Gujarat and Bundelkhand.

The Last Mughal Emperor

Bahadur Shah Zafar (1775-1862 CE) was the twentieth and last Mughal Emperor. He was a nominal emperor with no real power, as the British East India Company actually ruled India. He was a famous poet and patronised great poets like Mirza Ghalib, Ibrahim Zauq, Momin Khan Momin and Mustafa Khan Shefta. When the War of Independence broke out in 1857 CE, the people chose him as their emperor, but he was incapable of running the state affairs. The British sent him to Rangoon as a prisoner in 1858 CE; he died there in 1862 CE. With him, the Mughal Empire (1526-1857 CE) came to an end.

Why the War of 1857 Failed

The people could not succeed in the War of Independence 1857 CE because: (1) there was no united and capable central leadership; (2) the war was fought in separate regions without a common plan; (3) the British had better weapons, organisation, communication and resources; (4) many local rulers and groups did not join the war or supported the British; and (5) the freedom fighters lacked money and supplies. The war concluded in November 1858 CE.

Challenges Faced by the Muslims After 1857

After 1857 CE the Muslims faced severe challenges: (1) loss of political power, as the Mughal Empire ended and the British blamed the Muslims for the war; (2) ruin of their economic bases — the Muslims became landless and many lost their employment; (3) threat to the annihilation of Islamic culture; and (4) the Government of India Act 1858, under which the rule of the East India Company was abolished and India came directly under the British government, which adopted a policy of uneven treatment against the Muslims.

lessons.title: Reform Movements: Shah Waliullah and the Faraizi Movement
lessons.notes_html:
Why Muslim Rule Lasted for Centuries

Muslim rule in the subcontinent lasted for centuries (1206-1857 CE) because of: strong and organised administration set up by the Sultans and improved by Sher Shah Suri and Akbar; a sound land-revenue system; religious tolerance and policies like Akbar's Sulh-i-Kul, which won the support of non-Muslim subjects; powerful armies that defended the country against the Mongols; justice and welfare works such as roads, sarais and canals; and flourishing art, culture and trade.

Shah Waliullah Dehlavi (RA)

Shah Waliullah Dehlavi (1703-1762 CE) started his reform movement when despair was widespread amongst the Muslims because of anarchy and conspiracies, with Sikhs and Marathas as enemies of the Muslims. He identified that the Muslims had fallen because of political disunity and weakness, moral and social evils, and distance from the teachings of the Quran. As a remedy, he translated the Holy Quran into Persian so that Muslims could understand it, wrote 51 books in Persian and Arabic — the most famous being Hujjatullah-il-Baligha — tried to eradicate social evils, and persuaded Ahmad Shah Abdali to attack India to save the Muslims from the Marathas.

The Faraizi Movement

The Faraizi Movement was founded by Haji Shariatullah (1781-1840 CE) and was the most effective and popular movement of the Muslims in Bengal. Its purpose was to encourage the Muslims to follow the basic obligations of faith (faraiz) and to eliminate heresies. It supported the farmers against the suppressive behaviour of Hindu landlords and paid attention to the problems of the cultivators. After Haji Shariatullah, his son Dudhu Mian (Muhammad Hassan) continued the movement with the same objective. The movement empowered the Muslims to raise their voice against exploitation by Hindu landlords.

lessons.title: The Renaissance
lessons.notes_html:
What Was the Renaissance?

The word 'Renaissance' means 'rebirth' or 'revival'. It was a cultural and socio-political movement of the 15th and 16th centuries CE in Europe in which the learning, art and ideas of classical antiquity (ancient Greece and Rome) were rediscovered and revived. It started in Italy and then spread to all parts of Europe. The first and foremost factor of the Renaissance was the decline of feudalism.

Why Did It Begin in Italy?

Two main factors fostered the Renaissance in Italy: (1) The fall of Constantinople — the main cause — after which Greek scholars fled to Italy bringing classical texts and ideas of ancient Greece and Rome. (2) The wealth of Italian trade and the patronage of progressive rulers, popes and nobles — Italy's rich trading cities paid artists and scholars like Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael to work, so art and learning flourished there first. Other supporting factors were the decline of feudalism, the impacts of the Crusades, geographical voyages and the invention of the printing machine.

Great People of the Renaissance

  • Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519 CE) — Italian artist, scientist and inventor, a true 'Renaissance man'; he painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.
  • Michelangelo (1475-1564 CE) — sculptor, painter, architect and poet; famous for the statue of David, the Pieta, The Last Judgment and the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.
  • Raphael (1483-1520 CE) — painter and architect famous for harmonious composition and vibrant colouring; his famous work is The School of Athens.
  • William Shakespeare (1564-1616 CE) — the greatest writer in the English language and the world's greatest dramatist; famous plays include Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet, Othello, King Lear and Macbeth.
  • Saint Thomas More (1478-1535 CE) — English writer, lawyer and statesman, a great humanist who wrote Utopia.
  • Sandro Botticelli (1445-1510 CE) — Italian Renaissance painter of Florence, famous for The Birth of Venus and Primavera.

How the Renaissance Changed Thought

The Renaissance revolutionised European art and thought by reviving classical art and ideas. In art, painters and sculptors made realistic, human-centred works using harmony, proportion and vibrant colour. In thought, humanism placed man and reason at the centre; Shakespeare's plays centre on human character, emotions and individual choices — for example Hamlet's inner conflict, Othello's jealousy and Macbeth's ambition — and he used classical Greek and Roman stories and history. Scientists like Copernicus and Galileo questioned old beliefs with observation, laying the foundation of modern science. Thus Europe moved from blind faith towards reason, inquiry and creativity.

lessons.title: Exploration, Reformation and the Road to the Modern Age
lessons.notes_html:
The Age of Exploration

The Age of Exploration, also called the Age of Discovery, began in the 14th century CE and continued through the 16th century CE. The Mariner's Compass gave a great impetus to navigation, and European sailors searched for new sea routes to India and the Far East and discovered the Americas. Famous explorers were: Christopher Columbus (1451-1506 CE), an Italian explorer who made four voyages (1492-1504 CE) and discovered America in 1492 CE; Vasco Da Gama (1460-1524 CE), a Portuguese explorer who set sail from Lisbon in 1497 CE and became the first European to reach India by sea through the Cape Route; John Cabot (1450-1499 CE), who reached North America (Canada) in 1497 CE; Pedro Alvares Cabral (1467-1520 CE), the first European to reach the Brazilian coast in 1500 CE; and James Cook (1728-1779 CE), the British captain who explored New Zealand and Australia. The Age of Exploration led to European colonialism in Asia, Africa and America.

The Reformation

The Reformation (1517 CE) was begun by Martin Luther (1483-1546 CE), a German reformer, at Wittenberg. His movement split the Latin Christian church and reshaped religious and political institutions in Europe.

The Enlightenment

The Enlightenment Movement started in the 17th century CE and continued through the 18th century CE. It was an intellectual and cultural movement whose thinkers — such as Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau — emphasised reason over blind faith and superstition, so the 1700s are also called the Age of Reason. In science, Sir Isaac Newton (1643-1727 CE) reshaped natural philosophy with his work on gravity and the laws of motion.

The French Revolution

The French Revolution began in 1789 CE. It ended the monarchy in France and established democracy, liberty and equality. Together with the Renaissance, the decline of feudalism and of the Church's influence, the printing machine, exploration and trade, the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment, it shaped the Modern Era. The German philosopher Karl Marx also belongs to this modern age of new ideas.

lessons.title: Galileo and the Scientific Revolution
lessons.notes_html:
Galileo Galilei

Galileo Galilei (1564-1642 CE) was an Italian philosopher, astronomer and mathematician. He pioneered the use of the telescope in astronomy and supported the view that the planets revolve around the Sun. He discovered craters and mountains on the Moon, and he is known as the father of observational astronomy. Along with Nicolaus Copernicus, he brought a revolution in science during the Renaissance.

A New Way of Knowing

The Renaissance scientists questioned old beliefs with observation rather than blind faith. Copernicus and Galileo revolutionised astronomy; later, Newton's work on gravity and the laws of motion reshaped natural philosophy, and the Scientific Revolution fed into the Enlightenment — the Age of Reason — in which thinkers like Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau emphasised reason over superstition. This change in thinking is one of the main changes that shaped the Modern Era, along with the Renaissance, the printing machine, the Age of Exploration, the Reformation, the French Revolution and the Industrial Revolution.

Timeline of the Modern Period

  • 1453 CE — fall of Constantinople, a main cause of the Renaissance.
  • 1492 CE — Columbus discovered America.
  • 1517 CE — Martin Luther began the Reformation at Wittenberg, Germany.
  • 1698 CE — Thomas Savery invented the first steam engine.
  • 1760-1860 CE — the Industrial Revolution (began in Great Britain).
  • 1776 CE — Watt Steam Engine.
  • 1789 CE — the French Revolution began.
  • 1807 CE — Fulton's first successful commercial steamboat.

The Modern Period thus runs from the Renaissance (15th century CE) to the Industrial Revolution (19th century CE). Its important personalities include Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Shakespeare, Galileo, Newton, Rousseau, Adam Smith and Karl Marx.

lessons.title: The Industrial Revolution
lessons.notes_html:
What Was the Industrial Revolution?

The Industrial Revolution (about 1760-1860 CE) began in Great Britain in the late 18th century CE and changed production, transport and society through machines and steam power. Goods began to be produced quickly and cheaply by machines in factories instead of by hand at home.

Reasons Behind It

The factors behind the Industrial Revolution, as given in the chapter, were: (1) Capitalism — private owners had capital to invest in factories and machines. (2) European Imperialism — colonies supplied raw material and markets. (3) Mining of resources — coal and iron were available in large quantities. (4) The Steam Power Engine — a reliable source of power for factories, mines and transport. (5) The Agricultural Revolution — better farming produced more food and freed labour for factories. (6) The Scientific Revolution — new knowledge and inventions were applied to industry. (7) Governmental Policies — governments supported trade, industry and inventions.

Benefits

The benefits of the Industrial Revolution were: it developed the economy of the countries where it spread (England, Belgium, Germany, northern France, the USA and Japan); machines emerged and production increased greatly; mechanisation of agriculture improved farming and increased food production; communication and transportation improved dramatically through railways and steamboats; it increased employment opportunities, and factory wages were higher than farmers' earnings; populations migrated to urban areas and improvements were made in city planning; and new inventions such as the sewing machine, telegraph, light bulb and anaesthesia made life easier.

Disadvantages and Impact on the Subcontinent

There were also disadvantages: populations migrated in large numbers to urban areas, crowding the cities; hand-workers and cottage craftsmen lost their livelihoods because of mechanisation; factory work was long and hard; and coal-based industry polluted the growing industrial towns. In the subcontinent, which became a British colony, local handloom and cottage industries declined because they could not compete with cheap machine-made cloth; the subcontinent supplied raw material like cotton to British factories and became a market for British goods; new means of transport and communication — railways, steamboats and the telegraph — were introduced; and the economy became dependent on the colonial power.

How Colonialism Grew

First, in the Age of Exploration, European explorers found new sea routes. Then European nations — English, Dutch, French, Spanish and Portuguese — set up trading settlements and companies in Asia and Africa. As the Industrial Revolution created a hunger for raw material for factories and for markets to sell machine-made goods, trade turned into rule: these countries conquered, settled and governed huge parts of Asia and Africa as colonies, so raw material flowed to Europe and finished goods flowed back.

lessons.title: The Steam Engine
lessons.notes_html:
Power Before Steam

Before the steam engine, power came from water, wind, horses and men, which was unreliable. The steam engine uses hot steam from boiling water (heated by burning coal) to drive a piston back and forth, so factories could be located anywhere and large machines got reliable power.

The Inventors

  • Thomas Savery invented the first steam engine in 1698 CE, but it was not very useful.
  • Thomas Newcomen made the first practical fuel-burning engine in 1712 CE to pump water out of mines.
  • James Watt improved Newcomen's engine — the Watt Steam Engine of 1776 CE was smaller and more fuel-efficient, and was soon used in factories throughout England. The unit of power 'watt' is named after James Watt, and one horsepower equals 745.7 watts.
  • Richard Trevithick built the first steam locomotive to run on a track in 1804 CE.
  • Robert Fulton made the world's first commercially successful steamboat, the North River Steamboat (also called the Clermont), launched in 1807 CE; after it, steamboats became an important means of transport on rivers.

Results

Steam power was soon used in factories, mines and ships, and steam locomotives imported to the USA in 1829 CE led to railways. In this way the steam engine revolutionised transportation and industry, and became one of the most important inventions of the Industrial Revolution.
